title: Bitmasking for Subsets — Representing Sets as Integers
summary: Once a subset is an integer — bit i set means item i is in — enumerating every subset, checking membership, and building a dynamic-programming state all become integer operations. Small n only: the technique is exponential by construction.

slides.markdown:
A subset of a small collection can be represented as a single integer: bit `i` set means item `i` is in the subset, bit `i` clear means it isn't. Three items map to 3 bits, so `{A, C}` is the mask `101`, `{}` is `000`, and "everyone" is `111`.

Once a set is an integer, set operations become integer operations — union is OR, intersection is AND, and "is item i in this set" is a single AND-and-shift. That reframing unlocks two things interviewers care about: enumerating **every** subset of a small collection in a tight loop, and using a mask as the **state** in a dynamic-programming recurrence (think traveling-salesman-style problems over up to ~20 items).

The catch is right there in the setup: n items means 2ⁿ masks, so this only works while n is small — usually under 20.

slides.subTitle: And why that caps the technique to small n
slides.markdown:
With `n` items, each one is independently either in the subset or not — 2 choices per item, `n` items, so `2ⁿ` total subsets. That's the same count whether you enumerate them as bitmasks or generate them recursively; the mask is just the compact representation.

The growth is brutal past a small n: `2¹⁰ = 1,024`, `2²⁰ ≈ 1,000,000`, `2³⁰ ≈ 1,000,000,000`. An algorithm that iterates all subsets is doing real work at every one of those masks, so `n = 20` (a million subsets) is a comfortable interview-scale input, while `n = 30` is already pushing a second of pure iteration before you've done anything with each subset.

This is why bitmask techniques show up specifically on **small-n** problems — constraints like "n ≤ 20" in a problem statement are the interviewer telling you exponential-in-n is intended.

slides.sectionTitle: Every subset of {A, B, C} as a 3-bit mask
slides.markdown:
With 3 items — say `A` (bit 0), `B` (bit 1), `C` (bit 2) — every mask from `000` to `111` is a distinct subset:

`000` = `{}`, `001` = `{A}`, `010` = `{B}`, `011` = `{A, B}`, `100` = `{C}`, `101` = `{A, C}`, `110` = `{B, C}`, `111` = `{A, B, C}`.

Eight masks, eight subsets, matching `2³ = 8` — the empty set and the full set are both included, at masks `000` and `111`. The bit position is a fixed, arbitrary labeling (bit 0 is always "is A present"), and the *value* of the mask is what changes as you move through the subsets in the loop on the next slide.

<<< Image: a 2x4 or 1x8 grid of 3-bit binary strings from 000 to 111, each cell showing the mask alongside the subset of {A, B, C} it represents (e.g. 101 -> {A, C}), with bit 0 labelled A, bit 1 labelled B, bit 2 labelled C across the top >>>

Once you accept the mapping, enumerating every subset of `n` items is just counting from `0` to `2ⁿ - 1`:

```python
def all_subsets(items):
    n = len(items)
    for mask in range(1 << n):
        subset = [items[i] for i in range(n) if mask & (1 << i)]
        yield subset
```

`1 << n` computes `2ⁿ`. For each `mask`, checking `mask & (1 << i)` asks "is bit i set" — exactly the get-bit idiom from [bit idioms](bit-idioms). The inner loop over `i` costs `n`, so the whole enumeration is `O(n · 2ⁿ)` — fine for `n ≤ 20` or so, and the reason this technique doesn't scale past small n regardless of how tight the inner loop is written.

This single loop replaces what would otherwise be a recursive "include or exclude each item" backtracking function — same subsets, no recursion.

slides.sectionTitle: Iterating all submasks of a mask
slides.subTitle: Efficiently, not by re-checking every subset
slides.markdown:
A common follow-up: given one mask, enumerate only **its** submasks — subsets of the items it contains, not every subset of all `n` items. Checking every mask from 0 to `2ⁿ - 1` and filtering would waste time on masks that aren't submasks at all.

The standard trick walks submasks directly, largest to smallest, using a subtraction step:

```python
def submasks(mask):
    sub = mask
    while True:
        yield sub
        if sub == 0:
            break
        sub = (sub - 1) & mask
```

`(sub - 1) & mask` takes the next submask down: subtracting 1 borrows through the trailing zeros the same way it does in `n & (n-1)` from [bit counting](bit-counting), and ANDing with `mask` clips the result back to only the bits `mask` actually has set. This visits exactly the submasks of `mask`, not the full `0..2ⁿ-1` range.

slides.sectionTitle: Membership, add, and remove on a mask
slides.markdown:
Treating a mask as a set means the same three operations from get/set/clear apply directly, just read with set semantics instead of bit semantics:

- **Membership:** `mask & (1 << i)` — nonzero means item `i` is in the set.
- **Add:** `mask | (1 << i)` — union the set with `{i}`.
- **Remove:** `mask & ~(1 << i)` — intersect with everything except `{i}`.

These are exactly the get/set/clear idioms, renamed. What's new here is the vocabulary shift: once you're thinking "this integer is a set," `mask1 | mask2` reads as *union*, `mask1 & mask2` reads as *intersection*, and `mask1 & ~mask2` reads as *set difference* — three whole-set operations, each a single instruction, with no loop over elements at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Counting a subset's size for free
slides.markdown:
One useful side effect of the mask representation: "how many items are in this subset" is exactly `popcount(mask)` — the same Brian Kernighan bit-counting trick from the previous topic, applied to a set instead of a plain number.

This matters in problems that filter subsets by size — "find the largest subset satisfying some property" or "only consider subsets of size k" — because you get the size check for free from a mechanism you already have, rather than tracking a separate counter alongside every mask.

It's also a good sanity check while debugging: if you expect a mask to represent a 4-item subset and `popcount(mask)` comes back 3, you've mutated the mask incorrectly somewhere upstream.

The reason this technique earns its own topic instead of being a footnote on subsets: a bitmask is a **compact, hashable DP state**. Any recurrence of the shape "what's the best outcome given exactly this set of items used so far" can key its DP table on the mask directly — `dp[mask]` or `dp[mask][last]` — instead of a set data structure that's slower to hash and compare.

The canonical example is the **traveling salesman problem** on up to ~20 cities: `dp[mask][i]` means "minimum cost of a route that has visited exactly the cities in `mask`, ending at city `i`." Transitions move from `mask` to `mask | (1 << j)` for each unvisited `j` — exactly the add-item operation from two slides ago. Assignment-style problems (match `n` workers to `n` tasks) use the same shape.

The actual recurrence, base cases, and complexity analysis for bitmask DP belong in a dynamic-programming topic — the point to take from here is narrower: recognize a mask as a legitimate DP state the moment a problem's parameter is "which subset of small-n items have I used."

slides.sectionTitle: When n is too large for a bitmask
slides.markdown:
The failure mode is reaching for `1 << n` out of habit once n has grown past what a mask can carry.

- **n = 20** → about a million masks. Fine for a per-mask O(n) or O(n²) DP.
- **n = 30** → about a billion masks. Already too slow for anything beyond the most trivial per-mask work, and a `dp[mask][i]` table at this size is gigabytes.
- **n = 64** → the mask no longer fits in a standard 64-bit integer's usable range for some languages' signed-integer semantics, and `2⁶⁴` is astronomically larger than any real time budget regardless.

The tell that a problem *wants* bitmask DP is almost always in the constraints: `n ≤ 20` (sometimes stated as "number of cities/workers/items ≤ 20") is a strong signal, because `2²⁰ · n` or `2²⁰ · n²` both fit comfortably inside typical interview or contest time limits. If n is anywhere near 40+, the intended solution is something else entirely — greedy, a different DP dimension, or a polynomial algorithm — and forcing a bitmask onto it is a sign you've misread the constraint.

Both enumerate the same 2ⁿ subsets. They differ in constants and in what you get for free:

| Aspect | Bitmask loop | Recursive backtracking |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | `for mask in range(1 << n)` | Recurse: include item, exclude item |
| Per-subset cost | Fast — integer ops, no call overhead | Slower — function calls, stack frames |
| Early pruning | Hard — every mask is generated regardless | Natural — prune a whole branch by not recursing |
| Reuse as DP state | Direct — mask is already the state | Needs an explicit encoding to memoize |
| Readability for complex constraints | Gets awkward past simple include/exclude | Reads naturally with side conditions inline |

Use the bitmask loop when you'll touch every subset anyway or need the mask as a DP key. Prefer recursive backtracking when most branches get pruned early — for example, "stop as soon as the running sum exceeds a target" — because the mask loop cannot skip generating the masks it will never use.

slides.subTitle: A senior-level complexity nuance
slides.markdown:
A subtlety worth having ready: if you enumerate the submasks of **every** mask from 0 to `2ⁿ - 1` (not just one mask's submasks), the total work across all of them is **O(3ⁿ)**, not `O(4ⁿ)` as a naive "2ⁿ masks times up to 2ⁿ submasks each" estimate would suggest.

The reason: sum over every mask of its number of submasks equals, for each of the n bit positions, counting how many (mask, submask) pairs disagree in one of 3 ways at that position — both bits set, mask bit set and submask bit clear, or both clear (a submask can never have a bit the mask doesn't). Three choices per position, n positions, gives `3ⁿ` total pairs — this is the standard "sum over subsets" bound that shows up in bitmask-DP problems needing every mask's submasks (e.g. certain assignment and covering DPs).

`3²⁰ ≈ 3.5 billion` — noticeably worse than `2²⁰`, so a bitmask-DP transition that loops submasks of every mask needs its own budget check, separate from the plain `2ⁿ` enumeration cost.

A complete bitmask-subsets answer in an interview has a clear shape: notice the small-n constraint, map items to bit positions, state which operation you need — enumerate, check membership, or use the mask as DP state — and give the resulting complexity in terms of `2ⁿ` or `3ⁿ` explicitly.

That's the difference between "I'll use a bitmask" (a name-drop) and "n is at most 20, so I'll represent each subset as a 20-bit mask, iterate all `2²⁰` of them, and key a DP table on the mask directly since two equal masks are always the same state" — a complete argument an interviewer can follow end to end.

This closes out the bit-manipulation group: primitives, the four idioms, XOR's cancelling trick, fast bit counting, and now sets-as-integers — the same handful of operations, recombined at increasing scale.
